Let's try to detect covariate shift using PCA. PCA compresses the data into a lower-dimensional space, but this compression involves some information loss. This means that if we reconstruct the data from its compressed representation, the result won't exactly match the original data. The difference between the original data and the PCA reconstruction is called the reconstruction error.

The general idea is the following. We fit the PCA on a reference dataset R and measure the reconstruction error on data that the PCA never saw (a held-out part of R). If another dataset D has the same joint distribution as R, the PCA should reconstruct D about as well as it reconstructs the held-out R, so both errors will be similar. If the joint distribution has shifted, the directions learned from R no longer describe D well, and the reconstruction error changes.

One small caveat before we start, PCA only captures changes in means, variances and linear correlations, so a purely non-linear shift can go undetected.

Let's try to detect covariate shift using PCA. PCA compresses the data into a lower-dimensional space, but this compression involves some information loss. This means that if we reconstruct the data from its compressed representation, the result won't exactly match the original data. The difference between the original data and the PCA reconstruction is called the reconstruction error.

The general idea is the following. We fit the PCA on a reference dataset R and measure the reconstruction error on data that the PCA never saw (a held-out part of R). If another dataset D has the same joint distribution as R, the PCA should reconstruct D about as well as it reconstructs the held-out R, so both errors will be similar. If the joint distribution has shifted, the directions learned from R no longer describe D well, and the reconstruction error changes.

One small caveat before we start, PCA only captures changes in means, variances and linear correlations, so a purely non-linear shift can go undetected.
